text: Gradient descent updates model weights by stepping in the direction that most steeply reduces the loss, with the step size set by the learning rate.
Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in a neural network by applying the chain rule backwards through the layers.
Overfitting happens when a model memorises its training data instead of the pattern behind it, so training loss keeps falling while validation loss climbs.
Dropout randomly disables a fraction of neurons during training, which stops the network from leaning too heavily on any single pathway.
A convolutional layer slides a small learned filter across an image, which lets the same edge detector work no matter where the edge appears.
The attention mechanism lets a model weigh every other position in the input when encoding a token, which is how transformers handle long-range dependencies.
Batch normalisation rescales layer activations using batch statistics, which smooths the loss surface and allows a larger learning rate.
Cross-validation splits the data into folds and trains once per fold, giving a more reliable estimate of generalisation than a single holdout split.
An embedding maps a discrete token to a dense vector, placing items used in similar contexts close together in the vector space.
Reinforcement learning trains an agent through reward rather than labels, so the hard part is credit assignment across a long sequence of actions.
The bias-variance trade-off says a simple model misses real structure while a flexible one chases noise, and the best model balances the two errors.
Tokenisation splits raw text into the units a language model actually sees, and subword schemes let a fixed vocabulary cover words it never met in training.
A B-tree keeps data sorted in a shallow balanced structure, so a database can find any row in a handful of disk reads even across billions of rows.
A database index trades write speed and storage for read speed, which is why indexing every column makes inserts slow and queries no faster.
ACID transactions guarantee that a group of writes either all take effect or none do, even if the server loses power halfway through.
A write-ahead log records an intended change before applying it, so a crashed database can replay the log and recover a consistent state.
Normalisation removes duplicated facts from a schema, while denormalisation deliberately puts some back to avoid expensive joins on hot queries.
A query planner estimates the cost of different execution strategies and picks one, which is why stale table statistics can produce a terrible plan.
Sharding splits one logical table across many machines by a key, and a badly chosen key concentrates traffic on a single hot shard.
Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes for durability and read capacity, at the cost of replication lag between primary and replicas.
A hash join builds a hash table from the smaller relation and probes it with the larger one, which beats a nested loop when neither side is indexed.
Connection pooling reuses open database connections, because the handshake and authentication often cost more than the query itself.
An LSM tree buffers writes in memory and flushes sorted runs to disk, trading read amplification for very fast sequential writes.
Eventual consistency accepts that replicas disagree for a while, which is a reasonable trade when availability matters more than reading the newest value.
A light year is the distance light travels in a year, roughly nine and a half trillion kilometres, so it measures distance and not time.
A star spends most of its life fusing hydrogen into helium, and leaves the main sequence once the hydrogen in its core runs out.
A black hole forms when a massive star collapses so far that not even light can escape from inside its event horizon.
Redshift stretches the light of receding galaxies towards longer wavelengths, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it appears to recede.
The habitable zone is the orbital band where a planet could hold liquid water, which depends on how bright and hot its star is.
A supernova briefly outshines an entire galaxy and seeds surrounding space with the heavy elements forged in the dying star.
Tidal locking leaves one face of a moon permanently towards its planet, which is why we always see the same side of the Moon.
Astronomers find most exoplanets by watching a star dim slightly as a planet transits across it, repeating on a fixed period.
A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust, and the denser regions of one are where new stars condense under their own gravity.
Parallax measures stellar distance by the tiny shift in a star's apparent position as the Earth moves from one side of its orbit to the other.
The cosmic microwave background is faint radiation left over from the early universe, and its tiny temperature ripples trace the seeds of galaxies.
A telescope's resolving power grows with aperture, which is why large mirrors see finer detail than small ones regardless of magnification.
Browning meat before braising builds flavour through the Maillard reaction, which needs a dry surface and a pan hot enough to sear rather than steam.
Resting a roast after cooking lets the juices redistribute, so slicing it immediately spills onto the board what should have stayed in the meat.
Salting vegetables draws out water by osmosis, which is why salted cucumber slices go limp and release liquid within minutes.
Bread dough rises because yeast ferments sugars into carbon dioxide, and the gluten network traps those bubbles and holds the shape.
An emulsion suspends oil in water with the help of an emulsifier such as egg yolk, which is how mayonnaise stays thick instead of splitting.
Blanching vegetables in boiling water then chilling them in ice halts the enzymes that dull their colour and texture.
A roux of flour cooked in fat thickens a sauce, and the longer it cooks the darker and nuttier it tastes but the less it thickens.
Acid brightens a finished dish, so a squeeze of lemon at the end often fixes a soup that tastes flat despite enough salt.
Low slow heat turns tough collagen in cheap cuts into gelatin, which is why shoulder and shin reward hours of braising.
Cooking pasta in well-salted water seasons it from the inside, and the starchy cooking water helps a sauce cling to the noodles.
Caramelising onions takes far longer than most recipes claim, because the sugars only brown properly once the water has cooked off.
A sharp knife is safer than a dull one, since it cuts where you aim it instead of sliding off the skin of a tomato or onion.
Cadence is how many pedal revolutions you turn per minute, and most riders are most efficient somewhere between eighty and ninety.
Drafting behind another rider cuts the air resistance you face substantially, which is why a group travels faster than any of its members alone.
Correct saddle height leaves a slight bend in the knee at the bottom of the stroke, and a saddle set too high rocks the hips and strains the back.
Lower tyre pressure increases grip and comfort on rough roads, and beyond a point it rolls faster too because the bike stops bouncing.
Interval training alternates hard efforts with recovery, which raises the power you can sustain more quickly than steady riding alone.
A bike's gear ratio sets how far one pedal revolution carries you, so a smaller front ring makes a steep climb manageable.
Cleaning and lubricating a chain regularly costs minutes and saves a drivetrain, because grit held in old lubricant grinds down the cogs.
Climbing seated recruits different muscles than standing, and most riders save standing for the steepest ramps or to relieve stiffness.
Eating and drinking early on a long ride matters, since once you are depleted the stomach struggles to absorb enough to catch up.
Disc brakes keep their bite in the wet where rim brakes fade, which is the main reason they took over road bikes.
Cornering works best with the outside pedal down and the weight on it, looking through the turn to where you want to come out.
Recovery days are part of training rather than time off, because adaptation to hard efforts happens while you are resting.
A major scale has a fixed pattern of whole and half steps, which is why every major key sounds alike despite starting on a different note.
An interval is the distance between two pitches, and the perfect fifth sounds stable because the frequencies sit in a simple ratio.
A chord progression creates tension and release, and resolving the dominant back to the tonic is the oldest way of ending a phrase.
Minor keys sound darker than major ones mostly because the third of the scale sits a half step lower.
Syncopation places emphasis off the main beat, which is what makes a rhythm feel like it is pulling against the pulse.
A time signature says how many beats fill a bar and which note value counts as a beat, so the same melody feels different in three or four.
Modulation moves a piece into a new key, and a smooth modulation usually travels through a chord the two keys share.
Counterpoint weaves independent melodies that work together, so each line stands alone and the combination still makes harmonic sense.
Timbre is why a violin and a flute playing the same pitch sound nothing alike, and it comes from the pattern of overtones each produces.
An inversion rearranges which note of a chord sits lowest, which changes the colour of the harmony without changing the chord.
Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical steps, making every key equally usable and every interval slightly impure.
A pentatonic scale drops the two notes most likely to clash, which is why it is forgiving for improvising over a simple progression.
Most seedlings fail from too much water rather than too little, because waterlogged roots cannot take up the oxygen they need.
Compost improves both sandy and heavy clay soil, loosening the one and helping the other hold water and nutrients.
Mulch on a bed keeps moisture in the soil, holds the temperature steady and smothers the weed seeds that need light to sprout.
A plant label asking for full sun means six hours or more of direct light, and a tomato in deep shade will grow leaves but set little fruit.
Pinching out the growing tip of a young plant makes it branch sideways, trading height for a bushier shape and more flowers.
Hardening off moves seedlings outdoors gradually, because a plant raised in still warm air is easily killed by its first windy night.
Rotating crops between beds each year starves the pests and diseases that build up when the same family returns to the same soil.
Soil pH decides which nutrients a plant can actually absorb, so a deficiency sometimes means the wrong pH rather than missing fertiliser.
Deep infrequent watering encourages roots to grow downwards, while a daily sprinkle keeps them shallow and dependent.
Pruning a fruit tree in winter opens the canopy to light and air, which improves ripening and reduces fungal disease.
Companion planting pairs species that help each other, often by attracting the predators that eat the pests of their neighbour.
Perennials return each year from the same roots while annuals must be resown, which is why a perennial bed is cheaper over time.
A river delta forms where a river slows as it meets the sea and drops the sediment it has been carrying.
Mountain ranges create rain shadows: air rises and sheds its moisture on the windward slope and arrives dry on the far side.
Plate tectonics explains both earthquakes and mountain building, since most of each happens where two plates meet.
Ocean currents move heat around the planet, which is why some coastal cities are far milder than inland places at the same latitude.
A fjord is a glacial valley later flooded by the sea, which is why its walls are steep and its water unusually deep.
Time zones follow political borders as much as longitude, so a single wide country can insist on one clock throughout.
Deserts are defined by how little precipitation they receive rather than by heat, which is why Antarctica counts as one.
A watershed is the area draining into one river, so land use far upstream changes the water quality near the mouth.
Monsoons reverse direction seasonally as land heats and cools faster than the neighbouring ocean.
Map projections all distort something, and the familiar rectangular world map exaggerates the size of land near the poles.
Permafrost is ground frozen for years at a stretch, and thawing it destabilises anything built on top and releases trapped carbon.
An archipelago often traces a volcanic hotspot, with the islands ageing in sequence as the plate creeps over the plume.
